summary: Gives guidelines for designing RADIUS attributes, to help authors and reviewers within the IETF and other standards bodies. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules of thumb for people who invent new fields for a login-checking system, so the fields work well together.

subtitle: Rules of thumb for inventing new RADIUS attributes so that existing servers and clients can keep working.

tldr.problem: RADIUS attributes were being defined by many groups in inconsistent ways, with ambiguous data types, packed-together fields and attributes that quietly changed how the protocol works. That makes implementations complex and less interoperable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts attributes into basic and complex data types, recommends basic types, tells vendors and standards bodies to use the vendor space for their own attributes, and lists operational limits that new designs must respect. Appendix A turns this into a checklist.
tldr.outcome: Authors and reviewers get a shared yardstick. It is a Best Current Practice, so it does not update or deprecate existing standards. It has since been updated by RFC 6929 and RFC 8044.

today: RFC 6158 is a Best Current Practice that has been updated by RFC 6929 and RFC 8044, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Audience
sections.content:
RFC 6158 gives guidelines for designing attributes for the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service (RADIUS), both inside the IETF and in other Standards Development Organizations (SDOs). Authors are expected to check their drafts against it before requesting review, such as the Expert Review described in RFC 3575, and reviewers such as the AAA Doctors are expected to use it for consistency.

The document covers the art as well as the science of attribute design. It explains the trade-offs behind its advice, because there are few hard and fast rules. Section 2 states the guidelines, Section 3 gives the rationale, Appendix A repeats the guidelines as a checklist and Appendix B discusses existing attributes that do not follow them.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a how-to guide for people who add new fields to a login system, written so that different teams make fields that fit together.

sections.title: Where the Guidelines Apply
sections.content:
The advice applies to RADIUS attributes that carry service-provisioning, authentication or accounting data using the encodings in RFC 2865, RFC 2866 and later RADIUS RFCs. Because this is a Best Current Practice, it does not update or deprecate existing standards, and its uses of MUST and MUST NOT are limited to requirements already present in existing documents.

It is RECOMMENDED for all new RADIUS specifications, whether from a vendor, an SDO or the IETF. Specifications that ask for allocation in the standard space are expected to follow it or explain why they cannot. Vendors and SDOs MAY choose not to conform when their attributes are "not suitable for general usage", accepting limited interoperability.

Changes to the RADIUS protocol, or attributes such as Service-Type that in effect create new RADIUS commands, need deeper review and MUST NOT be undertaken outside the IETF. Reviews of standard-space attributes treat the guidelines as a checklist. Review of vendor-space specifications is optional but encouraged, since attributes not designed for general use can later spread widely; the RFC cites the Vendor-Specific Attributes of RFC 2548 in IEEE 802.11 access points.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are strongly suggested for anything meant for everyone. If a company is making a label only for its own gadgets, it can bend them, but it should know that it gives up working with other people's gear.

sections.title: Basic and Complex Data Types
sections.content:
RADIUS has no formal data definition language and does not send the data type on the wire. A client or server learns an attribute's type from its type code, using a pre-configured data dictionary. The RFC therefore splits formats into basic data types and complex data types.

Basic types include a 32-bit unsigned integer, enumerated values (a 32-bit integer with named values), an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, an IPv6 prefix, an Interface-Id (8-octet string), time as a 32-bit value in seconds since 00:00:00 UTC, January 1, 1970, a String of binary data and UTF-8 Text. String and Text are 253 octets or less, and less than that inside a Vendor-Specific Attribute (the rationale section gives 247 octets). Attributes needing more than 253 octets, such as EAP-Message, also count as basic, as do attributes grouped with the RFC 2868 tag mechanism, though that is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Everything else, including nested attributes, is a complex type and is NOT RECOMMENDED for normal use. Complex types MAY be used where they reduce complexity in non-RADIUS systems or where basic types would be awkward, and an explanation SHOULD be given for why one was chosen.

The reason is practical. A server can support a new basic-type attribute by editing its dictionary, but a complex type usually needs server code changes, and policy languages can rarely look inside sub-fields. Ad hoc parsing means more complex software and more room for bugs and security holes. Exceptions are authentication and security attributes, which need code changes on both ends anyway, and data the server can treat as opaque, such as EAP-Message, which SHOULD then be defined as a String that refers to an external document.

The tag scheme of RFC 2868 has only 31 tags, cannot nest, leaves only three bytes for tagged integers and is hard to use with arbitrary binary data. It is NOT RECOMMENDED as a generic grouping mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Plain boxes are easy: any guard can read a number, a name or an address. Boxes with little secret compartments inside need a special guard who has been trained for each one, so try not to make them.

sections.title: Standard Space and Vendor Space
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes three kinds of attribute. Single-vendor attributes belong in the vendor space, which a vendor controls through its Private Enterprise Number (PEN) in the Vendor-Id field. Attributes for an industry segment MUST be Vendor-Specific Attributes, managed by the SDO under the SDO's own PEN. Attributes of broad interest to the Internet community go in the standard space, allocated by IANA as described in RFC 3575.

The standard space is finite: it is limited to 255 attributes, and only about half remain available. Using type codes reserved for standard attributes without going through the IETF is called antisocial behavior and strongly discouraged. Vendors and SDOs SHOULD self-allocate from their own vendor space, and translating a vendor- or SDO-only specification into the standard space is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Inside the vendor space, the encoding of RFC 2865 Section 5.26 is expected. Implementations commonly use the Vendor Id as a key to the on-the-wire encoding, so a vendor SHOULD NOT use several encodings under one Vendor Id and SHOULD request one Vendor Id per encoding instead. Multi-vendor VSAs SHOULD be designed with the same care as standard attributes.

Vendor-space attributes must not change the operation of RADIUS, and servers that do not understand them MUST ignore them. The RFC notes this leaves room to build most things in the vendor space without losing functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one shared public bulletin board with only a few spots left, and every company also gets its own private board. Put things for everybody on the shared board, and put your own company's notes on your own board.

sections.title: Respecting the RADIUS Operational Model
sections.content:
New attributes have to fit the assumptions built into RADIUS. The protocol is stateless, apart from information passed with the State Attribute. Services are not provisioned in an Access-Reject or Disconnect-Request. Authorization checks are distinct from user authentication. Packets are authenticated and integrity protected. The protocol is request and response, and packet length is limited. Designs that need stateful behaviour without the State Attribute, or that provision services in an Access-Reject or Disconnect-Request, are called inherently incompatible with RADIUS and need to be redesigned.

An Access-Request that carries no user authentication attributes and no State Attribute is an authorization check. It gives no assurance that a live user exists, so attributes with confidential content, such as Tunnel-Password, should be barred from responses to such checks. One request solicits at most one response, and changing that model is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The maximum RADIUS packet length is 4096 octets, so designers SHOULD NOT assume larger packets can be processed. Even smaller packets can exceed the Path MTU and be fragmented, and fragmented UDP is poorly tested on network devices, so messages should be kept small. For data that might not fit, three approaches are RECOMMENDED:

  1. A sequence of packets, such as Access-Request and Access-Challenge exchanges, with a clear way to signal how attributes are split.
  2. Names instead of values, as Filter-Id refers to a pre-provisioned set of filter rules.
  3. As a last resort, Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (RFC 4821), which is not generally applicable.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the guard's habits are fixed. The guard does not remember you between visits, answers one question with one answer, and uses small notes. Your new form has to work with those habits instead of breaking them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
New data types mean new code, and new code can bring new bugs and attack vectors. RADIUS servers are highly valued targets because they control network access and talk to databases of usernames and passwords; in the extreme, a flaw in a complex type could let an attacker take complete control of the server. Opaque data does not remove the threat, it moves it to the system that consumes the data, so that system SHOULD be isolated from RADIUS and run with minimal privileges.

For cryptography, new attributes SHOULD support algorithm negotiation and MUST specify a mandatory-to-implement algorithm, ideally one certifiable under FIPS 140. The MD5-based obscuring of User-Password (RFC 1321) and SHA-1 are under scrutiny, and using them in new attributes is NOT RECOMMENDED. Clients SHOULD include a Message-Authenticator attribute in every Access-Request.

The RFC states plainly that the security of the RADIUS protocol is in general poor, and that robust deployments SHOULD support a secure protocol such as IPsec. It also says that ignoring the guidelines may lead to ambiguous protocol decoding, lost billing information and denial-of-service attacks. The IANA section asks IANA to do nothing, but provides guidelines for the Expert Reviewers appointed under RFC 3575.
sections.plainLanguage: Every new kind of form means new rules for the guards to learn, and every new rule is a place where a trickster might sneak in. So keep forms simple, and keep anything that handles mystery envelopes locked away from the guard's main office.

sections.title: The Design Checklist and Existing Complex Attributes
sections.content:
Appendix A restates the guidelines as questions grouped under headings such as types matching the RADIUS data model, improper data types, vendor-specific formats, changes to the operational model and allocation of attributes. For example, it asks whether the data fits the basic types, and if so says it SHOULD use one of them in a standard attribute or VSA.

Appendix B reviews older attributes that do not follow the guidelines, including CHAP-Password, CHAP-Challenge, Tunnel-Password, ARAP-Password, ARAP-Features, Connect-Info, Framed-IPv6-Prefix, Egress-VLANID, Egress-VLAN-Name and the Digest-* attributes. For each it explains why a complex type is acceptable or how it could have been defined using basic types.
sections.plainLanguage: At the back there is a yes-or-no list to check your idea against, and a list of old forms that broke the rules, with notes on why.

items.title: Dictionary edit
items.text: A server supports a new basic-type attribute by adding a dictionary entry, with no code change.

items.title: Less special parsing
items.text: Separate attributes avoid attribute-specific parsing and reuse validation for well-known types.

items.title: Easier data entry
items.text: Administrators can enter well-known types more easily than complex structures.

items.title: Smaller attack surface
items.text: New data types need new code, which may add new bugs and attack vectors.
